questions_asked: For peak-hour driving on these highways, do traffic volumes arrive as a fairly even steady stream, or do they come in noticeable bursts or waves of cars?
When self-driving cars coordinate with each other, does the main gain come from smoother, steadier flow, or from letting them run faster?
For planning whether to add a dedicated self-driving lane, roughly what change in delay or throughput do you need before it is worth it?
expert_answers: Peak-hour traffic on these highways is not a steady even stream. It arrives in noticeable bursts and waves: platoons of vehicles form behind slower or merging traffic, and flow fluctuates on time scales of seconds to minutes. This is a well-established empirical feature of congested freeway traffic (the "stop-and-go" wave phenomenon), and it is strongest precisely at peak hours when volume approaches capacity. On a coarser scale, arrivals also vary over the peak period itself (a ramp-up, a plateau, and a decline), but the burstiness relevant to car-following and cooperation modeling is the short-time-scale platooning.

The main gain comes from smoother, steadier flow, not from higher speed.

Coordinated self-driving cars mainly reduce the spacing (headway) they need between vehicles and damp out the stop-and-go waves that waste capacity. That lets more vehicles pass a given point per hour at roughly the same or slightly higher speed. The capacity benefit is fundamentally a density/headway effect, not a speed effect.

Running faster is a secondary and largely self-limiting gain: free-flow speed is capped by road geometry, speed limits, and safety, and raising speed actually reduces achievable density. So the dominant mechanism is smoothing flow and tightening headways, which is why the payoff shows up as increased throughput and reduced delay rather than shorter free-flow travel times.

A dedicated lane is worth it only if the throughput or delay gain to the remaining general-purpose traffic is large enough to offset the capacity you remove from it. As an empirical planning rule: dedicating a lane takes roughly 20–33% of capacity off a 3–5 lane road, so you need the self-driving lane to carry enough vehicles to more than compensate — typically the gain must be on the order of 10–20% or more in total corridor throughput (or an equivalent delay reduction) before it clearly pays off. Below roughly 10%, the loss of a general-purpose lane usually cancels the benefit. This is a judgment range, not a precise figure; the exact threshold depends on the self-driving share and how much headway tightening is actually achieved.
